passage: Zainab saw it from the next bench in the village school's hall: Aditi, her best friend since Class 1, tucked a folded slip under her palm and copied the last two answers of the science paper. Nobody else noticed. All the way home along the canal path, Zainab's stomach twisted. Aditi kept talking about the buffalo calf as if nothing was wrong. At the tamarind tree, Zainab stopped. "I saw you today. The slip." Aditi went pale. "Please don't tell." "I'm not going to shout it," said Zainab. "But go to Sir yourself, before results. I can't pretend it didn't happen." Aditi kicked a stone and said nothing. "I'll wait for you at the gate tomorrow," Zainab added, and walked on, unsure whether they were still friends.

qa.q: Where did Zainab tell Aditi she had seen the slip?
qa.a: At the tamarind tree on the canal path home.

qa.q: What was Zainab feeling as she walked home, and what does it show?
qa.a: She felt torn between loyalty and honesty. Her stomach twisted, and she was unsure at the end whether they were still friends.

qa.q: What was wise in how Zainab responded to Aditi?
qa.a: She spoke privately, refused to pretend it hadn't happened, and urged Aditi to go to the teacher herself rather than joining in or staying silent.

qa.q: How might Aditi have felt when Zainab spoke to her?
qa.a: Frightened and ashamed. She went pale, begged Zainab not to tell, and kicked a stone in silence.

grounding: The protagonist knows her best friend cheated, urges her privately to come clean and refuses to be complicit.

passage:
Counsellor's note.

Sonali came to see me on Monday. Last week she reported to her teacher that a group of friends had shared answers during the unit test. Since then the group has stopped talking to her, and Saurabh, who she considered her closest friend, walked past her in the corridor. She said she feels like a traitor. I noticed she kept her voice level and did not blame anyone loudly, and she did not regret it, but she was lonely. I told her that acting on a principle can cost belonging, and that this hurts. We discussed spending time with people who share her values. She agreed to join the library club and will come back next week.

qa.q: What did Sonali report to her teacher last week?
qa.a: That a group of friends had shared answers during the unit test.

qa.q: How does Sonali feel about what she did, and what is the evidence?
qa.a: She feels like a traitor and lonely, but she does not regret reporting. She kept her voice level and did not blame anyone loudly.

qa.q: What did the counsellor suggest Sonali do?
qa.a: Accept that acting on principle can cost belonging, stay steady, and spend time with supportive people, starting with the library club.

qa.q: How might Saurabh see Sonali's report?
qa.a: Possibly as a betrayal, since he walked past her in the corridor. He may be angry or ashamed, but the note does not say.

grounding: The protagonist reports cheating and loses friends, and is helped to accept the cost and seek supportive people.

passage:
"Gopika, just show me question five. Please."
"Arnab, I can't. It's a test."
"You're so selfish. Everyone shares."
"I'm not sharing, and I'm not trying to be mean."
"Priya said you'd say that. She said you think you're better than us."
"I don't. I'm tired of feeling guilty for saying no, though." She breathed out. "Look, I'll study with you after school today. We can go through the chapter together, and you can ask me anything before the test."
"That's not the same."
"I know. But it's what I can do."
Arnab scowled and turned away. Gopika's hands were shaking, but she stayed where she was and opened her notebook.

qa.q: Which question did Arnab want Gopika to show him?
qa.a: Question five.

qa.q: How does Gopika feel about refusing, and what shows it?
qa.a: She feels guilty and nervous but firm. She says she is tired of feeling guilty for saying no, and her hands were shaking.

qa.q: What did Gopika offer instead of sharing answers?
qa.a: To study with Arnab after school, going through the chapter together so he could ask her anything before the test.

qa.q: Why might Arnab react with anger even though Gopika offered help?
qa.a: He wanted the answers now, and studying is more work. He may also be afraid of failing, so he scowled and turned away.

grounding: A classmate is pressured to share answers, refuses kindly, offers to study together and accepts some anger.

passage: I'm Elizabeth, and I still remember the afternoon Anjali told me at the tea stall near school. She was pale. "I copied off Meera's paper in the history test. Promise you won't tell." I didn't know what to say. I felt honoured that she trusted me and also uneasy. I didn't call her a bad person, because I knew she was scared. But I also said, "I can't say it's okay. And I won't lie for you if someone asks." She looked hurt. I told her the best way to fix this was to go to the teacher, and that I'd walk her to the staffroom if she wanted. She didn't that day. Two days later she went, and I waited outside on the bench.

qa.q: Where did Anjali tell Elizabeth about the test?
qa.a: At the tea stall near school.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth feel when Anjali confided in her?
qa.a: Honoured that Anjali trusted her but also uneasy, since she knew it was wrong and did not want to lie for her.

qa.q: What would you advise someone whose friend confides that they cheated?
qa.a: Listen without judging, say plainly that you can't approve, don't act as their alibi, and encourage them to fix it, maybe by offering to go with them. 🙂

qa.q: How might Anjali have felt on hearing that Elizabeth would not lie for her?
qa.a: Hurt and maybe frightened, since she looked hurt. Later she went to the teacher with Elizabeth waiting outside, so she may have felt supported too.

grounding: A friend confides cheating and asks for secrecy; the protagonist listens, refuses to be an alibi and encourages her to fix it.

passage:
Mr Nair walked in with the marked papers and said, "Two of you copied on the last question. I want to know who." Nobody breathed. I glanced at Ujjwal, who sits beside me. He stared at his desk and did not say a word, and neither did anyone else. After the bell the whole class was whispering names in the corridor, but Ujjwal didn't join in. He stayed behind. I saw him talking quietly with Mr Nair by the window for a few minutes. I don't know what they said, and Ujjwal didn't tell me. Nobody was called out in class. I can't say what he was feeling, but he looked tired when he came out.

Kishore

qa.q: What did Mr Nair say when he came in with the marked papers?
qa.a: That two of them copied on the last question and he wanted to know who.

qa.q: What could Kishore tell about Ujjwal's feelings, and what could he not tell?
qa.a: Ujjwal looked tired afterwards, which suggests the situation weighed on him, but Kishore can't know his thoughts or what was said.

qa.q: Why was Ujjwal's way of handling the question wise?
qa.a: He did not gossip or lie outright, and he spoke to the teacher privately, weighing fairness to honest students against loyalty.

qa.q: How might the honest students in the class see what happened?
qa.a: Possibly with relief that the matter went to the teacher, since fairness matters to them. Nobody was named in class, so they may also feel unsure.

grounding: A teacher asks who cheated; the protagonist avoids gossip and speaks privately with the teacher, seen by an observer.

passage:
Monday. When the coach announced Indu as captain, Vaibhav clapped and smiled and felt as if he'd swallowed a stone. He had wanted it since Class 8. In the group chat he typed "She's good at speaking, not sure about tactics" and then deleted it.

The next Saturday. He watched Indu at practice: she arrived early, learned the juniors' names, changed the drill when someone struggled. It irritated him. It also, unwillingly, taught him something.

Three weeks later. He told his brother, "I'm jealous." It was easier to say aloud. That evening he stayed after practice to work on his passing, and asked Indu to time him.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav type in the group chat and then delete?
qa.a: "She's good at speaking, not sure about tactics".

qa.q: What was Vaibhav feeling when the coach announced Indu as captain?
qa.a: Envy and disappointment. He smiled and clapped but felt as if he'd swallowed a stone, since he had wanted the role since Class 8.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav do that helped him move forward?
qa.a: He admitted his jealousy to his brother, studied what Indu did well and kept practising, instead of sabotaging her or spreading doubts.

qa.q: How might Indu feel when Vaibhav asks her to time him?
qa.a: Probably surprised and pleased. It is a sign of respect, and it may show her that he has accepted the situation and wants to work together.

grounding: A rival gets the captaincy the protagonist wanted; he admits the envy, learns from her and keeps working.

passage: Diary. Manjula here, 9:40 pm. I heard Shreya's name in assembly again, this time for topping the mock test, and my whole body went hot. I didn't hear the rest of the announcement. All day I replayed things she has said, even things from last year. In maths I did four questions in an hour because I was busy being angry. At home I picked up my phone and started to type something mean about her to the class group, then stared at it for ages. I deleted it. Then I noticed something: I'd spent the whole day thinking about her, not about my own chapters. She isn't even here, and she's controlling my day. Tomorrow I'll make a plan for my own revision and keep her name out of it.

qa.q: When did Manjula write her diary entry?
qa.a: At 9:40 pm.

qa.q: Why did Manjula delete the message she started to type, and what did she realise about her anger?
qa.a: She stopped herself from hurting Shreya's reputation, and realised her hatred was tying her energy to Shreya so that Shreya was controlling her day.

qa.q: What would you advise Manjula to do next?
qa.a: Shift her focus to her own revision plan and goals, as she intends, and if the anger stays strong, talk it through with someone she trusts.

qa.q: How might Shreya see the situation?
qa.a: She may not know Manjula is angry at all, since the diary says Shreya isn't even there. She is probably just enjoying her result.

grounding: The protagonist cannot bear a rival's name, sees hatred tying her energy to the rival and shifts to her own goals.

passage: Diary, Friday. Chandrika here. Debate finals today and Amandeep beat me by two points. I wanted to be furious, and I was for about ten minutes, then I remembered his last rebuttal. It was so clever that I actually wrote it down. We walk the same way home so we ended up together, arguing about the topic all over again and laughing. Tanvi teased, "Are you two friends now?" and for a second I nearly said "no, he's just competition." I didn't. I said, "He's good, and that's why I have to work harder." I think that's true. Next round I want to beat him. And I want him there, because he makes me better. 🙂

qa.q: By how many points did Amandeep beat Chandrika?
qa.a: By two points.

qa.q: Why did Chandrika almost say Amandeep was "just competition" to Tanvi, and why didn't she?
qa.a: She feared looking soft in front of a teasing friend, but she admired his work and knew the friendship was real, so she told the truth.

qa.q: How can rivalry help both people, according to Chandrika?
qa.a: It pushes each to work harder, as she says Amandeep makes her better, and she does not need to hide their friendship to compete.

qa.q: How might Amandeep see Chandrika after that walk home?
qa.a: Probably as both a challenger and a friend. They argued and laughed together on the way, so he likely enjoys the contest too.

grounding: Two rivals compete fiercely yet admire each other; the protagonist acknowledges the friendship and uses the rivalry as a push.

passage: Ten minutes to the relay. Damini was tying her spikes at the edge of the Aizawl track when Lalremsiami strolled over, ribbon still around her neck. "Beat you in the 200 by a whole second. Maybe next time try running?" A few girls giggled. Damini's face went hot and she wanted to fire something back. But the relay was coming and she needed her legs, not a fight. She looked up. "Congratulations. You ran well." Then she turned and walked to her lane. It stung the whole way. She fixed her eyes on the baton in her hand and thought, one second, I can find one second. She ran her leg clean and quick, and she took the sting home with her as a plan.

qa.q: How long before the relay did Lalremsiami come over to Damini?
qa.a: Ten minutes.

qa.q: What did Damini want to do at first, and why did she not do it?
qa.a: She wanted to fire something back, but the relay was coming and she needed her energy for it, not a fight.

qa.q: What did Damini do that showed a wise way to handle a boasting rival?
qa.a: She stayed composed, congratulated her briefly and used the sting as fuel by focusing on finding one second, instead of trading insults or hiding away.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami have felt when Damini congratulated her?
qa.a: Possibly disappointed not to get a reaction, or perhaps a little embarrassed at how her boast landed. Damini's calm reply gave her nothing to argue with.

grounding: A rival boasts about beating the protagonist, who stays composed, congratulates briefly and uses the sting as fuel.

passage: In the school hall, when the principal announced Sumit as winner of the science fair, applause filled the room. He looked for Urmila in the third row, his old project partner from Class 8, and found her clapping without looking at him. Later, at the display tables, she left as he approached. He felt a prickle of hurt. When he thanked the judges, he said, "Urmila's idea about the water sensor is why it works." The next day, he waited by the library door and said once, "I didn't want this to come between us. If you want to talk, I'm around." Urmila nodded slowly and said, "Maybe. Give me time." He didn't push, and walked to class.

qa.q: Which project idea did Sumit credit to Urmila?
qa.a: The water sensor.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling when Urmila left as he approached, and how did he respond?
qa.a: He felt hurt, but he stayed gracious. He shared credit with Urmila and reached out to her once instead of flaunting his win or pretending he did not care.

qa.q: What would you advise Sumit to do now?
qa.a: Give Urmila time, avoid flaunting the win, and stay friendly without pushing.

qa.q: How might Urmila see Sumit's win?
qa.a: Possibly with mixed feelings, such as pride in her own idea and pain at watching him win alone. She clapped without looking at him, but she also said "Maybe. Give me time."

grounding: The protagonist wins and a former friend turns cold; he is gracious, shares credit and reaches out once.
